cards.title: Dhu l-Qarnayn Building the Iron and Molten Brass Gate Against Gog and Magog
cards.note: Surah 18:92–98 depicts Dhu l-Qarnayn erecting a rampart of iron blocks and molten brass between two mountain cliffs to seal in Gog and Magog until the apocalyptic promise of the Lord, matching the sixth-century Syriac Alexander Legend.

discussion.view: Classical commentators such as Ibn Ishaq, al-Tabari, and al-Qurtubi identify Dhu l-Qarnayn as Alexander the Great (`al-Iskandar`) or a righteous world-conqueror who built an iron-and-brass barrier in the north.
discussion.reply: Historical records of Alexander of Macedon (356–323 BC) show a polytheistic Greek king who built no apocalyptic wall against Gog and Magog. The plot of a two-horned monotheistic king traveling to the ends of the earth and casting an iron-and-brass gate between two mountains against Gog and Magog was composed in Syriac in northern Mesopotamia shortly before Islam.

cards.title: Iblis Refusing to Prostrate to Adam Because Fire Surpasses Clay
cards.note: Surah 7:11–18 narrates God commanding the angels to prostrate before Adam and Iblis refusing because he was created from fire whereas Adam was created from clay, matching the Latin Vita Adae et Evae 13–16 and the Syriac Cave of Treasures.

discussion.view: Muslim commentators present the command for the angels to bow to Adam and Iblis's boast of fiery origin over clay as the primeval account of Satan's fall at the dawn of creation.
discussion.reply: Genesis 1–3 contains no command for angels to bow to Adam and no dialogue with Satan about fire and clay. The narrative of God commanding the angels to worship the newly formed Adam comes from the apocryphal Life of Adam and Eve (Vita Adae et Evae 13–16), and Satan's specific boast that he is 'fire and spirit' refusing to bow to 'a thing of dust' appears in the Syriac Cave of Treasures.

He was not one of those who prostrated themselves. [12] He said, ‘What kept you from prostrating yourself when I commanded you?’ He said, ‘I am better than him. You created me from fire, but You created him from clay.’ [13] He said, ‘Go down from here! It is not for you to be arrogant here. Get out! Surely you are one of the disgraced.’ [14] He said, ‘Spare me until the Day when they are raised up.’ [15] He said, ‘Surely you are one of the spared.’ [16] He said, ‘Because you have made me err, I shall indeed sit (in wait) for them (on) Your straight path. Whoever of them follows you – I shall indeed fill Gehenna with you – all (of you)!’

cards.title: Waking After Centuries and Sending an Ancient Silver Coin to Buy Bread
cards.note: Surah 18:19–20 recounts the youths waking in their cave, supposing they slept a day, and sending one companion with their silver coin (`wariqikum`) to the city to buy food discreetly, matching the Syriac and Latin Seven Sleepers of Ephesus homilies.

discussion.view: Classical commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir recount that the Companions of the Cave fled an idolatrous Roman emperor and were miraculously preserved in sleep for over three centuries as a sign of bodily resurrection.
discussion.reply: The narrative of Christian youths hiding in a cave near Ephesus under Emperor Decius (AD 249–251), waking under the Christian emperor Theodosius II (AD 408–450), and sending a companion into town with obsolete silver coins was a famous fifth- and sixth-century Christian hagiography preserved in the Syriac homilies of Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) and Gregory of Tours.

cards.quranEn: [19] So We raised them up (again) that they might ask questions among themselves. A speaker among them said, ‘How long have you remained (here)?’ Some said, ‘We have (only) remained (here) a day, or part of a day.’ Others said, ‘Your Lord knows how long you have remained (here). So send one of you with this paper (money) of yours to the city, and let him see which (part) of it (has the) purest food, and let him bring you a supply of it. But let him be astute, and let no one realize (who) you (are). [20] Surely they – if they become aware of you – they will stone you, or make you return to their creed, and then you will never prosper.’

sources.en: One of the youths, named Yamlikhā, goes down to the city to assess the situation and buy food. cards.title: Crucifixion Substitution: They Did Not Kill Him, It Seemed So to Them
cards.note: Surah 4:157–158 states that Jesus was neither killed nor crucified, 'rather it was made to appear so to them (`shubbiha lahum`),' matching the docetic substitution accounts in Irenaeus (Against Heresies 1.24.4) and the Nag Hammadi treatises.

discussion.view: Classical Sunni commentators such as al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God cast the physical likeness of Jesus onto another person—such as a disciple or an enemy—who was crucified in his place while Jesus was raised bodily to heaven.
discussion.reply: First-century Christian, Jewish, and Roman sources (the Gospels, Paul, Tacitus in Annals 15.44, and Josephus in Antiquities 18.3.3) record Jesus's crucifixion under Pilate. The claim that a look-alike substitute was crucified while Jesus ascended unharmed originated in second-century Gnostic texts (Basilides in Irenaeus 1.24.4; Second Treatise of the Great Seth), which denied that a spirit could suffer in flesh.

cards.title: Moses, His Young Servant, and the Salted Fish Reviving at the Spring
cards.note: Surah 18:60–65 narrates Moses and his young servant traveling to the junction of the two seas, where their dried fish revives and swims away into the water, matching the revived salted fish in Jacob of Serugh's Alexander discourse.

discussion.view: Muslim commentators and hadith (Sahih al-Bukhari 122) explain that Moses and his attendant Joshua set out with a salted fish in a basket as a divine sign to locate the sage al-Khidr at the meeting of the two seas.
discussion.reply: The Torah records the life of Moses and Joshua without any journey to the junction of two seas or a revived fish. In Late Antiquity, the episode in which a traveler's cook washes a dried salted fish at the Fountain of Life and watches it come to life and escape belongs to the Alexander Romance tradition, preserved in the Syriac discourse of Jacob of Serugh (d. AD 521; cf. the spring-washing variant in Talmud Tamid 32b).

cards.quranEn: [60] (Remember) when Moses said to his young man, ‘I shall not give up until I reach the junction of the two seas, or (else) I shall go on for a long time.’ [61] When they reached the junction of them, they forgot their fish, (for) it had taken its way into the sea, swimming off. [62] So when they had passed beyond (that place), he said to his young man, ‘Bring us our morning meal. We have indeed become weary from this journey of ours.’ [63] He said, ‘Did you see when we took refuge at the rock? Surely I forgot the fish – none other than Satan made me forget to remember it – and it took its way into the sea – an amazing thing!’ [64] He said, ‘That is what we were seeking!’ So they returned, retracing their footsteps. [65] And they found a servant, one of Our servants to whom We had given mercy from Us, and whom We had taught knowledge from Us.

cards.title: Dhu l-Qarnayn Reaching the Muddy Spring of the Setting Sun and the East
cards.note: Surah 18:83–91 narrates Dhu l-Qarnayn ('The Two-Horned One') traveling to the sun's setting place in a muddy spring and to its rising place over a shelterless people, matching the journeys of Alexander the Great in the Syriac Christian Legend.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record early reports identifying Dhu l-Qarnayn as a righteous world-conqueror granted divine pathways across the earth, explaining 'setting in a muddy spring' as either how the western ocean appeared to his eye or the sun's literal western station.
discussion.reply: In the early seventh-century Syriac Christian Legend Concerning Alexander, Alexander prays to God as the king upon whose head God placed two horns to thrust down the kingdoms of the world, marches to the fetid western sea where the sun enters the window of heaven, and travels east to the people who have no shelter from the rising sun's heat.

cards.quranEn: [83] They ask you about Dhū-l-Qarnayn. Say: ‘I shall recite to you a remembrance of him. [84] Surely We established him on the earth and gave him a way of access to everything. [85] He followed (one such) way of access [86] until, when he reached the setting of the sun, he found it setting in a muddy spring, and he found next to it a people. We said, “Dhū-l-Qarnayn! Either punish (them) or do them (some) good.” [87] He said, “As for the one who does evil, we shall punish him. Then he will be returned to his Lord, and He will punish him (with) a terrible punishment. [88] But as for the one who believes, and does righteousness, for him (there is) the good payment, and we shall speak to him something easy from our command.” [89] Then he followed (another) way of access [90] until, when he reached the rising (place) of the sun, he found it rising on a people for whom We had not provided any shelter from it. [91] So (it was), but We had already encompassed what his situation was in (our) awareness.

cards.title: Surah 38 Account of God's Two Hands Forming Clay Adam and Iblis's Boast
cards.note: In Surah 38:71–85, God asks Iblis why he refused to prostrate before 'what I created with My two hands,' and Iblis boasts that he was made from fire while Adam was made from clay, matching the Syriac Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–15.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir state that God honored Adam by fashioning him from clay with His two hands and commanding the angels to perform a prostration of honor, which Iblis rejected through analogical pride comparing fire to clay.
discussion.reply: Distinctive to Surah 38 is God's rebuke concerning 'what I created with My two hands' alongside Iblis's fire-over-clay argument. Genesis 1–3 contains no angelic prostration to Adam, whereas the Syriac Cave of Treasures depicts God fashioning Adam with His holy hands and the fallen prince refusing to bow because he is fire and spirit while Adam is dust, alongside Vita Adae et Evae 14–15.

cards.quranEn: [71] (Remember) when your Lord said to the angels: ‘Surely I am going to create a human being from clay. [72] When I have fashioned him, and breathed some of My spirit into him, fall down before him in prostration.’ [73] So the angels prostrated themselves – all of them together [74] – except Iblīs. He became arrogant, and was one of the disbelievers. [75] He said, ‘Iblīs! What prevented you from prostrating yourself before what I created with My two hands? Have you become arrogant, or are you one of the exalted?’ [76] He said, ‘I am better than him. You created me from fire, but You created him from clay.’ [77] He said, ‘Get out of here! Surely you are accursed! [78] surely My curse (is going to remain) on you until the Day of Judgment.’ [79] He said, ‘My Lord, spare me until the Day when they are raised up.’ [80] He said, ‘Surely you are one of the spared [81] – until the Day of the known time.’ [82] He said, ‘Then, by Your honor, I shall indeed make them err – all (of them) [83] – except for Your devoted servants among them.’ [84] He said, ‘(This is) the truth, and the truth I say: [85] I shall indeed fill Gehenna with you and those of them who follow you – all (of you)!’

cards.title: Rival Claims Over Whether the Sleepers of the Cave Were Seven or Eight
cards.note: Surah 18:22 catalogues rival claims over the headcount of the youths in the cave (three, five, or seven with their dog as the eighth), mirroring the split between eight youths in Jacob of Serugh's Syriac homily and seven youths with a dog in Theodosius.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir report from Ibn 'Abbas that Christian denominations of Najran and Syria disputed whether the sleepers numbered three, five, or seven alongside their dog Qitmir, and that 18:22 endorses the count of seven youths plus their dog.
discussion.reply: Late antique Christian sources preserve the exact numerical divergence cited in 18:22: West-Syrian bishop Jacob of Serugh (d. 521) consistently numbers the youths of Ephesus as eight companions in his Syriac memra, whereas the Greek and Latin tradition represents them as seven brothers, to whom the sixth-century pilgrim Theodosius (De situ terrae sanctae 26) adds the dog Viricanus at their feet.

cards.quranEn: Some say, ‘(There were) three, the fourth of them was their dog.’ But others say, ‘(There were) five, the sixth of them was their dog’ – guessing about what is unknown. Still others say, ‘(There were) seven, the eighth of them was their dog.’ Say: ‘My Lord knows about their number. No one knows (about) them except a few.’ So do not dispute about them, except (on) an obvious point, and do not ask for a pronouncement about them from any of them.

cards.title: Iblis Refusing to Bow to Adam Formed from Dry Clay and Dark Mud
cards.note: Surah 15:26–42 contrasts creating man from sounding dry clay of dark molded mud (salsalin min hama'in masnun) with creating the jinn from scorching fire before Iblis refuses to bow to Adam, matching the Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–16.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir interpret salsalin min hama'in masnun in 15:26–33 as dried clay formed from dark, altered mud that makes a ringing sound when struck, contrasting Adam's earthen origin with the smokeless scorching flame of the jinn.
discussion.reply: Surah 15 is the sole Quranic passage to use the formula 'dry clay from dark molded mud' (salsalin min hama'in masnun) and 'fire of scorching wind' (nar al-samum). The narrative structure — God breathing His spirit into clay-formed Adam, the angels bowing, Iblis refusing to worship a creature of dust, and his banishment until the appointed time — parallels the Syriac Cave of Treasures and Vita Adae et Evae 14–16.

cards.quranEn: [26] Certainly We created the human from dry clay, from molded mud, [27] and the (ancestor of the) jinn, We created him before (that) from scorching fire. [28] (Remember) when your Lord said to the angels: ‘Surely I am going to create a human being from dry clay, from molded mud. [29] When I have fashioned him, and breathed some of My spirit into him, fall down before him in prostration.’ [30] So the angels prostrated themselves – all of them together [31] – except Iblīs. He refused to be with the ones who prostrated themselves. [32] He said, ‘Iblīs! What is (the matter) with you that you are not with the ones who prostrated themselves?’ [33] He said, ‘I am not (one) to prostrate myself before a human being whom you have created from dry clay, from molded mud.’ [34] He said, ‘Get out of here! Surely you are accursed! [35] Surely the curse (is going to remain) on you until the Day of Judgment.’ [36] He said, ‘My Lord, spare me until the Day when they are raised up.’ [37] He said, ‘Surely you are one of the spared [38] – until the Day of the known time.’ [39] He said, ‘My Lord, because You have made me err, I shall indeed make (things) appear enticing to them on the earth, and I shall indeed make them err – all (of them) [40] – except for Your devoted servants among them.’ [41] He said, ‘This is the straight path (incumbent) on Me. [42] Surely My servants – you will not have any authority over them, except for whoever follows you of the ones who are in error.

cards.title: Surah 2 Account of the Angels Bowing to Adam After the Naming Scene
cards.note: Immediately after Adam recites the names of all things before the angels in 2:31–33, Surah 2:34 narrates God commanding the angels to prostrate before Adam while Iblis refuses in arrogance, matching Vita Adae et Evae 13–15 and the Cave of Treasures.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that in 2:34 God commanded the angels to bow to Adam as a greeting of honor after Adam demonstrated superior knowledge by naming the creatures, whereas Iblis refused out of envy and pride.
discussion.reply: Unlike 7:12, 15:33, and 38:76, which give Iblis's fire-versus-clay argument, 2:34 places the command to prostrate immediately after Adam's naming of the creatures (2:31–33) and attributes Iblis's refusal simply to arrogance (istakbara). This sequence directly parallels the Syriac Cave of Treasures, where Adam names all creatures on his throne before the angels bow the knee and the rebellious archangel refuses.

cards.quranEn: (Remember) when We said to the angels, ‘Prostrate yourselves before Adam,’ and they prostrated themselves, except Iblīs. He refused and became arrogant, and was one of the disbelievers.

cards.title: The Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim Sealed in Sleep for Years
cards.note: Surah 18:9–12 introduces the youths of the Cave and al-Raqim (the inscription) whose ears are sealed in sleep for generations before awakening, matching Gregory of Tours' account of the lead tablets placed at the sealed entrance of the Ephesian cave.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir record multiple early explanations of al-Raqim in 18:9, with Ibn 'Abbas, Sa'id ibn Jubayr, and Wahb ibn Munabbih identifying it as an inscribed tablet of stone or lead recording the names and story of the youths at the cave entrance.
discussion.reply: Distinctive to 18:9–12 is the pairing of 'the Companions of the Cave and al-Raqim' (ashaba l-kahfi wa-l-raqim) with the sealing of their ears in sleep. In the sixth-century Passio Septem Dormientium of Gregory of Tours (translated from Syriac), two Christians named Theodore and Ruben write the history of the youths on lead tablets and place them inside the blocked mouth of the cave.

cards.quranEn: [9] Or did you think that the companions of the cave and al-Raqīm were an amazing thing among Our signs? [10] (Remember) when the young men took refuge in the cave, and said, ‘Our Lord, grant us mercy from Yourself, and furnish the right (course) for us in our situation.’ [11] So We sealed up their ears in the cave for a number of years, [12] and then We raised them up (again), so that We might know which of the two factions would better count (the length of) time (they had) remained (there).

sources.en: When the emperor was informed that they were staying in this cave, he ordered that the mouth of the cave be blocked off. cards.title: Believing Youths Standing Before the Pagan Ruler and Fleeing to the Cave
cards.note: Surah 18:13–16 narrates how the believing youths stood up to proclaim that their Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth, rejected their people's idols, and withdrew into the cave, matching Gregory of Tours' account of the youths defying Decius.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir recount that the youths were noble sons of Ephesus who stood before the idolatrous king Daqyanus (Decius), refused to offer pagan sacrifices, and fled to a mountain cave outside the city to preserve their faith.
discussion.reply: Whereas 18:9–12 summarizes the sleep in the cave and 18:17–20 describes their awakening and silver coin, 18:13–16 focuses on their public confession before the pagan court (idh qamu fa-qalu Rabbuna Rabbu l-samawati wa-l-ard). Gregory of Tours' sixth-century Latin Passio (translated from a fifth-century Syriac original) opens with the noble youths arrested before Emperor Decius, refusing pagan sacrifice, and retreating to the cave.

cards.quranEn: [13] We shall recount to you their story in truth: Surely they were young men who believed in their Lord, and We increased them in guidance. [14] We strengthened their hearts, when they stood up and said, ‘Our Lord is the Lord of the heavens and the earth. We do not call on any god other than Him. Certainly we would then have spoken an outrageous thing. [15] These people of ours have taken gods other than Him. If only they would bring some clear authority concerning them! Who is more evil than the one who forges a lie against God? [16] When you have withdrawn from them and what they serve instead of God, take refuge in the cave. Your Lord will display some of His mercy to you, and will furnish some relief for you in your situation.’

sources.en: During the reign of the emperor Decius there was a persecution against the Christians. At that time seven men from prominent families, named Maximianus, Malchus, Martinianus, Constantinus, Dionysius, Johannes, and Serapion were arrested and investigated before the emperor. Although threatened and ordered to sacrifice to the pagan gods, they refused. (3) They were granted some time to think and change their minds, while the emperor visited another city; they sold their possessions and gave the proceeds to the poor, and withdrew to a cave on Mount Celion, selecting Malchus to go in secret to the city to purchase supplies. (4) When they learned that the emperor, on his return, had asked about them, they became scared and prayed, and God set them in a deep slumber.

cards.title: The Resurrection Proof and Building a Sanctuary Over the Sleepers' Cave
cards.note: Surah 18:21 states that the sleepers were discovered to confirm the resurrection of the dead, after which the authorities resolved to build a sanctuary (masjidan) over their cave, matching Gregory of Tours' Passio on Emperor Theodosius II.

discussion.view: Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain that God caused the citizens to discover the youths so the king and his divided subjects would know that bodily resurrection is true, after which the prevailing party built a sanctuary over the cave entrance.
discussion.reply: Surah 18:21 preserves two specific narrative elements from the Christian legend of Ephesus: first, that the awakening took place specifically to settle a theological controversy over the bodily resurrection under Emperor Theodosius II; and second, that after the youths fell asleep again, the authorities proposed building a shrine or basilica (basilica magna) directly over their bodies at the cave.

cards.quranEn: So We caused (the people of the city) to stumble upon them, in order that they might know that the promise of God is true, and that the Hour – (there is) no doubt about it. When they argued among themselves about their situation, they said, ‘Build over them a building. Their Lord knows about them.’ Those who prevailed over their situation said, ‘We shall indeed take (to building) a place of worship over them.’

sources.en: Then Maximianus said that therefore all should believe in the resurrection of the dead, after which the saints lay down again and slept upon the earth. The Emperor saw these things and crying placed his own clothes over the martyrs and ordered golden coffins to be made for them. But that night the saints appeared to him and told him to leave them above the ground. Then Theodosius constructed a great church (basilica magna) above them, and there made a hospice (receptaculum) for the poor. And, when the bishops had assembled, he celebrated their feast.
